title: REBEKAH AGREED TO MARRY A MAN SHE HAD NEVER MET
paragraphs: REBEKAH AGREED TO MARRY A MAN SHE HAD NEVER MET

She left home with a stranger, traveled toward a future she could not see, and answered one terrifying question with two Hebrew words that changed the direction of her life: “I will go.” But the deepest lesson of her story is not about recklessness, romance, or blindly following feelings. It is about what faith looks like when God has made the next step clear but has not shown you everything waiting at the end of the road.
There is a moment in Genesis 24 that is so quiet you can almost miss how enormous it is.
A young woman is simply asked a question.
And her answer changes her life.
Abraham is old. Sarah has died. Isaac, the promised son through whom God had said Abraham's offspring would be named, still has no wife.
Abraham sends his servant back toward his relatives with an extraordinary assignment: find a wife for Isaac.

He does not merely wander into town hoping chemistry will do the rest. He asks the LORD for guidance. At the well, he asks God for a particular confirmation involving hospitality—not merely a woman willing to give him water, but one willing to water his camels as well.
She does what the servant had prayed about.
The servant discovers that she belongs to Abraham's extended family.
And suddenly an ordinary trip to a well becomes part of something far larger than Rebekah could have imagined when she walked out carrying her water jar.
That alone should make somebody reading this stop.
Because you do not always recognize a turning point while you are standing inside it.
Sometimes destiny does not announce itself.
Sometimes it looks like another morning.
Another act of kindness nobody applauds.
Another ordinary moment in which you simply choose to be faithful.
Rebekah did not wake up knowing that before long she would be asked to leave everything familiar.
Maybe that is where this story finds you.
You keep wondering when God is going to do something dramatic, while God may already be shaping your future through the ordinary obedience you almost dismissed as insignificant.
Then the conversation reaches Rebekah's family.
The servant explains what happened. The family recognizes God's providence in the circumstances. Gifts are exchanged. Morning arrives.
And suddenly the possibility becomes painfully real.
Rebekah's brother and mother want her to remain for a while.
No demand that she meet Isaac first.
No recorded request to inspect the property.
No guarantee that the journey will be comfortable.
No photograph of Isaac tucked inside the servant's belongings.
But we need to be careful here, because Scripture deserves more than inspirational exaggeration.
Rebekah was not recklessly marrying a random stranger who appeared at a well.
Genesis gives us a much richer context.

Abraham's servant had specifically sought God's direction. Rebekah's identity had been established. Her family had heard the servant's account and recognized the LORD's hand in what had happened. The marriage arrangement existed within the kinship and cultural world of the patriarchal period. And critically, Genesis 24:57–58 actually records Rebekah being consulted before the immediate departure.
“Make enormous decisions without wisdom because Rebekah did.”
“If circumstances line up, God must be promising you the outcome you want.”
Scripture never gives us permission to turn providence into superstition.
What Genesis gives us is something more demanding.
Rebekah had enough light to take the next step...
but not enough light to see the whole journey.
And maybe that is exactly where your faith has been hurting.
God has given you the next faithful step.
You want to know how everything ends before you obey.
You want God to explain why the door closed.
Why the prayer has taken so long.
Why doing what was right did not immediately make life easier.
Why you had to release something you loved.
Why you are walking through a chapter you never would have written for yourself.
But biblical faith has never meant possessing tomorrow.
It means trusting the God who does.
Rebekah climbed onto a camel without knowing every detail awaiting her.
Every mile increasing the distance between the woman she had been and the life awaiting her.
There must have been moments when the silence became loud.
Will I ever see home again?
Scripture does not tell us precisely what Rebekah thought on that road, so we should not pretend it does.
But Scripture does tell us she went.
Faith can look like moving forward because the God who has proven faithful is worthy of trust even when you cannot yet see what waits beyond the horizon.
And this is where Rebekah's story becomes uncomfortable for us.
Because many of us say we trust God when what we actually trust is explanation.
We trust God when the numbers work.
We trust God when everyone agrees.
We trust God when obedience produces immediate relief.
We trust God when the relationship survives.
We trust God when the diagnosis changes.
We trust God when the money arrives.
We trust God when the prayer is answered exactly as requested.
But when God remains God and refuses to hand us the entire script...
And sometimes heaven's answer is simply enough grace for today.
Rebekah's אֵלֵךְ — “I will go” confronts that demand for control.
Not because Christians should become careless.
But because there comes a point after prayer, Scripture, wisdom, discernment, and genuine conviction when endless delay can disguise itself as caution.
Sometimes we are not waiting for guidance anymore.
We are waiting for a guarantee.
And God never promised that obedience would come with one.
Maybe your hardest surrender right now is not something sinful.
Maybe it is your insistence on knowing.
Knowing whether you will ever get back what obedience costs you.
Rebekah did not know the whole story.
And what Rebekah certainly could not have understood in full was how her marriage would become woven into the covenant story stretching far beyond her lifetime.
Isaac and Rebekah would become the parents of Jacob.
From Israel would come the tribes.
Through Judah's line, generations later, would come Jesus the Messiah according to the flesh.
Suddenly Genesis 24 is not merely a romantic story about a woman finding a husband.
It sits inside the unfolding history of God's covenant purposes that ultimately lead us toward Christ.
Because the Bible is not fundamentally a collection of inspirational stories telling you how to become the hero.
Its great story moves toward God's saving work.
Isaac is not Jesus in Genesis 24.
And we should resist forcing every small feature of this chapter into a hidden allegory the text itself does not explicitly establish.
But from our place later in redemptive history, we can see something Rebekah could not see from her camel:

God was carrying His covenant promises forward through real human decisions, imperfect families, painful chapters, unexpected meetings, marriages, births, failures, mercy, judgment, and grace until, in the fullness of time, Jesus Christ came.
That should encourage the person who thinks his or her small obedience cannot possibly matter.
You cannot see everything God sees.
But there is another reason we must not romanticize her.
Her story did not become perfect after Genesis 24.
Because some people have been taught a Christianity where obedience supposedly earns a painless life.
Rebekah would experience infertility before conceiving.
There would be conflict between the sons in her womb.
There would be favoritism in the family.
Eventually deception would enter the household.
Genesis 27 records Rebekah participating in the scheme by which Jacob deceived his father Isaac and obtained the blessing intended for Esau.
The woman who once said, “I will go,” would later make profoundly complicated and morally troubling choices.
That is important because Scripture does not airbrush its people.
The Bible refuses to manufacture saints out of flawless marble.
Used by God and still desperately in need of grace.
Maybe your story began with beautiful faith too.
Maybe there was a time when you could say “I will go” without hesitation.
You manipulated an outcome because waiting for God became unbearable.
You tried to force what you believed had been promised.
You became someone your younger self would barely recognize.
And now you read stories about faith and quietly disqualify yourself.
“If people knew what happened in my marriage...”
“If they knew how angry I am at God...”
“If they knew how far I wandered...”
“If they knew how many times I promised Jesus I would stop...”
The Gospel was never written for people who successfully kept their lives spotless.
The scandal is not that broken people need grace.
The scandal is how stubbornly we keep pretending we don't.
We hide because we think Jesus is waiting for the cleaned-up version of us.
Meanwhile the cross announces something devastatingly different.
You could not clean yourself enough.
Jesus did not die because humanity needed motivational improvement.
Our rebellion against God is not cosmetic damage.
And Christ did what we could never do.
He went willingly toward the cross.
Grace does not tell you that your sin does not matter.
The cross proves that it matters more than we wanted to admit.
Grace tells you that Jesus is greater.
Maybe that is the real question underneath Rebekah's ancient question.
Not, “Would you marry someone you have never met?”
That is not what God is asking you to imitate.
When Jesus calls you away from sin and toward Himself...
When Christ exposes the secret you keep defending...
When repentance means deleting what keeps dragging you back...
When He tells you that you cannot save yourself...
When grace stands before everything you have done and tells you there is forgiveness through Christ...
There is an enormous difference between blind faith and biblical faith.
Christian faith is not believing without reason in a nameless unknown.
And maybe somebody reading this has spent years near Christianity without actually surrendering to Christ.
People may even assume you are spiritually strong.
But underneath all of it, Jesus has been standing at the door of the part of your life you refuse to surrender.
Your religious vocabulary belongs to Him.
And Jesus does not merely ask to decorate the life you have already chosen.
He calls us to deny ourselves, take up our cross, and follow Him.
The version of Christianity where Jesus is Savior whenever you need rescue but never Lord when He commands surrender.
Maybe you have spent years asking Jesus to bless the road you chose when what He has been asking is whether you will follow Him onto His road.
And tonight your answer does not need to sound impressive.
It may come from somebody who has failed a hundred times.
But perhaps your prayer needs to become:
Because salvation is by grace, and the grace that saves us does not leave us comfortably enslaved to the sin from which Christ came to redeem us.
That is the Gospel Warrior message.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
Not by editing your history until it looks respectable.
He tells the truth about sin.
He forgives those who come to Him.
He takes stories we thought were finished and begins writing redemption where we expected only shame.
And maybe this article reached you because you needed to remember something.
Your worst chapter does not outrank the cross.
Your failure is not more powerful than Christ's mercy.
Your past cannot travel backward and undo Calvary.
If you belong to Jesus, your identity is not finally determined by the ugliest thing you have done.
It is determined by the Savior to whom you belong.
And if this exposed something you have been hiding, do not write an impressive comment.
There may be another believer reading the comments who has survived the valley you are entering.
There may be someone who needs to know they are not the only Christian still fighting.
Your honesty may become somebody else's permission to stop pretending.
Not because clicking “Share” earns favor with God. It doesn't.
The Gospel cannot be bought, and God's grace is not for sale.

But if Christ has given you something worth proclaiming, supporting faithful Gospel work can be one practical way of helping biblical encouragement reach another exhausted believer, another wandering son, another ashamed daughter, another person silently wondering whether Jesus could possibly want them back.
If you want to glorify God through what you share online, use that space intentionally.
Send it privately to the person who would never comment publicly but whom you know is struggling.
So if money is tight, keep your money.
It is seeing sinners turn toward Christ and believers grow deeper in Him.
Rebekah's road began with an ordinary day at a well.
Miles later, Genesis says she lifted her eyes.
There was a man walking in the field.
The man she had never met was no longer somewhere beyond the horizon.
And Genesis 24:67 closes this extraordinary journey with something remarkably tender.
Isaac took Rebekah as his wife.
The road she could not see had reached the place God already knew.
Your story will not duplicate Rebekah's.
God has not promised every Christian a spouse, an easy ending, financial prosperity, freedom from suffering, or the earthly outcome we imagine.
But if you are in Christ, He has promised something infinitely greater than a comfortable script.
So perhaps faith tonight is not demanding to see the ending.
Perhaps it is opening your trembling hands.
Perhaps repentance is finally releasing the thing you have protected from Jesus.
Perhaps obedience is taking the next faithful step Scripture has already made clear.
Perhaps grace is discovering that after everything you have done, Christ is still calling sinners to come.
And perhaps the sentence you will remember tomorrow is not about Rebekah at all.
You do not need to see the whole road when you know the One who holds you on it.
Then follow where His Word leads.
Share what could help someone find Him.
Save what you may need to read again.
Because somewhere between the well and the horizon, Rebekah discovered what every surrendered heart eventually learns:
Sometimes the road God asks you to walk begins before He lets you see where it ends—but no surrendered step taken in faithfulness to Him is invisible to the God who already sees the whole road.
